newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTORCYCLING - DOOHAN KEEPS HIS HEAD AND WINS AHEAD.
newsitem.headline: MOTORCYCLING - DOOHAN KEEPS HIS HEAD AND WINS AHEAD.

text.p: Australian world champion Michael Doohan won a fourth straight Italian 500cc motorcycling Grand Prix on Sunday after avoiding the mishaps that befell his rivals.

The win was in fact the Australian's fifth consecutive victory at the Mugello racetrack north of Florence -- he won the San Marino Grand Prix here in 1993 -- and took his career 500cc tally to 37, level with the late Mike Hailwood.
That made him equal second in the all-time list, still well behind Italian Giacomo Agostini's 68 wins.
Doohan finished a comfortable 10.056 seconds clear of Yamaha's Italian Luca Cadalora, who staged a remarkable fightback before his home crowd from 16th on lap one.
It was the first time this season a 500cc bike other than a Honda has been in the top three.
Japan's Nobuatsu Aoki was third on a Honda.
Doohan leads the standings on 95 points, ahead of Spain's Alex Criville on 78.
Criville, the only other winner this season, was fourth after running through a gravel trap.
The race was a procession for the last eight laps as the three times world champion secured his third victory in four races this season.
But he could count himself lucky before that.
Japan's Tadayuki Okada led after the first lap before Doohan, working up from fourth place, slipped by his team mate in the fourth lap. Okada retook the lead in the sixth.
Doohan then led from the seventh until the 11th when the Japanese passed him again and almost took both out as the Australian battled to get back in front once more.
Okada lost his balance, flipping out of the saddle and over the handlebars, landing on his boots beside the bike and still hanging on.
Somehow he kept the machine and himself upright before managing to sling his leg back over the saddle and continue to the pits.
He then retired with a dislocated wrist.
"It was quite a heart-stopping moment," said Doohan. "It took me about another lap to get it together again. I was going past him and he was all over the top of the bike."
"It was close to 200kph and I was right behind him," he said.
After taking what he called a one lap "concentration break", Doohan settled down with no further risks.
"The motorcycle's a very good bike but it still needs a bit of tender loving care to get it round," he said.
Japan's Takuma Aoki was the main rival in second place from lap 11 to 16 but he then crashed out.
While luck smiled on Doohan, not that he needed any, Criville had a nightmare day. He broke his Honda on the warm-up lap and had to use a spare bike with different settings.
Criville had been second after the first lap but, after the ninth lap error, found himself fighting back from 12th.
Italians won the earlier two lower categories, with three times world champion Max Biaggi taking the 250cc honours in a scrap to the line.
Biaggi and compatriots Loris Capirossi and 40-year-old wild card Marcellino Lucchi all led during the race. At the finish, the three were almost level.
In the 125cc class, 18-year-old Italian Valentino Rossi won and took the overall lead by one point after his third win in four races this season.
He celebrated by riding around the circuit standing in the saddle and brandishing a life-size inflatable doll in his arms and on his shoulders along with the Italian flag.
Unfortunately, the doll, pressed on Rossi by exuberant fans, did not like his embrace or the bike's exhaust.
"I had a problem with her. She deflated," he said.
